newsitem.title: JAPAN: Landing on disputed isle embarrasses Japan PM.
newsitem.headline: Landing on disputed isle embarrasses Japan PM.

text.p: The Japanese government moved swiftly on Tuesday to distance itself from a nationalist legislator who earlier landed on one of a group of islands in the East China Sea claimed by Japan, China and Taiwan.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was among the first to repudiate Shingo Nishimura, a member of the main opposition New Frontier Party (Shinshinto), who with three other people surveyed and held a brief ceremony on one of the Senkaku Islands, known in Chinese as the Diaoyu Islands.

"It is well-known that the owner of the land has refused to allow landings there. Do members of parliament have the right to completely ignore that?" a clearly displeased Hashimoto told reporters in parliament.

Other top officials appealed for calm over the decades-old dispute, which last year exploded into fiery anti-Japanese demonstrations in Hong Kong and Taiwan after a Japanese right-wing group built a small lighthouse on one of the islands.

"The government will calmly deal with the issue, as countries which are taking standpoints different from Japan are also dealing with it calmly," Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told a news conference.

The Hashimoto government's spokesman, Seiroku Kajiyama, told a news conference that while the islands were Japanese territory, the group's actions were "extremely regrettable" and should not be allowed to damage Japan-China relations.
Nishimura's group sailed on a chartered vessel carrying cameras, video recording equipment and a Japanese flag, his parliamentary office said in a statement.
"We believe this landing on the Senkaku Islands will be the starting point for an awakening of national consciousness and the rebirth of a Japan with pride," the statement said.

Nishimura's statement pointedly challenged the central government, which has sought to insulate Japan's complicated relations with China from the dispute over the uninhabited islands, which lie 1,600 km (1,000 miles) southwest of Tokyo.
"The Senkaku Islands are indisputably Japan's territory. It is a matter of course that a member of parliament should survey Japanese territory," the statement said.
The landing party included a local Okinawa politician, Hitoshi Nakama, whose landing on the island last month Tokyo officials lamented as a possible provocation to China.
The Senkaku issue languished for decades, obscure to all but maritime law experts and small bands of nationalists on both sides of the dispute until the construction of the lighthouse last July.
That drew a flotilla of vessels in the months that followed carrying Taiwanese and Hong Kong Chinese protestors, several of whom briefly landed on the Japanese-administered islands.
Last September, a Hong Kong activist drowned when he jumped into stormy waters near the islands to press China's claim.

In response to recent reports in Hong Kong media that new groups of Chinese activists would try to visit the islands later this month, the Japanese Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday the government would repel future landing attempts on the island.
In February, Japan sent a letter to U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan in which it sought to have Tokyo's official stance on the islands included in a U.N. report on the Law of the Sea.
China says its ownership of the islands dates back to ancient times.
